text:
You were born in Toronto to Ana and Carlos Moreira, both teachers who believed in hard work and quiet dignity. You were expected to be smart, and you were—sharp, quick with numbers, always the first to raise your hand. But what began as confidence curdled early into certainty, and certainty into the unshakable belief that you were *right*, not just often, but *always*.  

You called it clarity. You called it responsibility. You called it love.  

You met Elena at university. She was studying architecture, wore her black hair short, laughed like she surprised herself. You loved her for her precision, the way she drew clean lines on paper and lived by them. You believed you could build something true with her. You did—for a while. You married. You had a son, Mateus. You believed you were building a family, but what you were really building was a hierarchy—with you at the top, because only you saw things clearly.  

When Mateus was seven, he was diagnosed with autism. The doctors used words like *spectrum*, *support*, *early intervention*. You refused to accept it. You said the school was lazy, the doctors overeager, the diagnosis a shortcut. You believed—no, you *knew*—that with enough discipline, Mateus could be “normal.” You called it high expectations. You called it love.  

Elena fought you. She said, “This isn’t about you being right. It’s about Mateus being safe.” You told her she was coddling him, that her softness would ruin him. You took over his schedule—rigid routines, no stimming, no retreat into his own world. When he melted down, you called it “manipulation.” When he stopped speaking for three days, you said he was “testing boundaries.”  

Elena left. She took Mateus and moved in with her sister, Catarina. You called it betrayal. You told everyone—your friends, your parents, even your priest—that you were the one who truly loved Mateus, that you were the only one strong enough to prepare him for the real world.  

You kept visiting. You brought flashcards, math drills, eye-contact exercises. Mateus would shut down. You saw defiance, not pain. Elena begged you to stop. You said, “Someone has to care enough to be hard on him.”  

Ten years passed. Mateus was seventeen. He had stopped speaking to you altogether. Elena still let you visit, hoping for reconciliation, but every time, you brought your methods, your charts, your certainty.  

Then came the winter night you drove to their house in Brampton. Mateus had been acting out, Elena said—withdrawn, aggressive. You said, “He needs structure. He needs to know we won’t let him fail.”  

You went into his room. You found him curled in the corner, humming, rocking. You turned on the lights. You knelt, too close, and said, “Look at me, Mateus. Look at me. You are stronger than this. You are not broken.”  

He screamed. A sound you’d never heard—raw, animal, endless.  

Elena ran in. She shoved you back. “Get out! You don’t see him! You never have!”  

You stood, coat half-on, and said, “I’m the only one who sees him clearly.”  

You drove home. You told yourself you were the martyr, the one who loved enough to be hated. You believed it. You had to.  

That night, you took a bottle of wine and drove to the old overlook on the escarpment. You didn’t know why you went. To think. To feel the cold. To be alone with your righteousness.  

The car skidded on black ice. You remember the guardrail rushing toward you, then nothing—  

—and in the last second, not fear, but fury: *It isn’t fair*.  

You died still certain you were right.  

And that was the sin. Not the love. Not the care. But the unshakable, all-consuming pride that let you call cruelty clarity, control love, and blindness—vision.  

You named it duty.  

But it was pride.  

And it cost Mateus his father, Elena her husband, and you—everything.  

The engine cuts. The lights go out.  

Darkness.

You were born in Bristol, and your mother, Margaret, used to say you had a face that showed your thoughts too clearly. You never liked that about yourself—how your envy made your jaw tighten, your smile go thin. You thought it made you ugly. But you never said so.

You envied Laura from primary school because she could run fast without trying. You envied Sarah from university because her parents paid for her flat while you worked three jobs. But it wasn’t until you met David at the library archives in 1998 that envy became a weapon.

David was a historian, soft-spoken, with a habit of tapping his pen twice before writing. You were both researching local textile mills. You published a paper first—on women’s labor in 1830s Manchester—but David’s came out six months later, nearly identical in structure, with better sources. It won the Thwaites Prize. You didn’t. You told yourself it didn’t matter. But it did.

You began watching David. You learned he met his wife, Clara, every Thursday at 6:15 at the Turkish café on Whiteladies Road. You learned he kissed her hand when she arrived. You learned she was a pianist, that they had no children, that she wore her dark hair in a loose bun.

You started going to Clara’s concerts. You sat in the third row, left side. You studied how the light caught her hands, how she never turned a page wrong. After the third concert, you approached her. You said, “I’m a colleague of David’s. I admire your work.” You smiled the way your mother taught you—small, closed, safe.

Clara invited you for tea. You went. You complimented her Shetland shawl. You asked about her practice schedule. You said, “David never talks about you.” That was the first lie. You said it lightly, like a joke. But Clara’s smile dimmed.

You kept seeing her. Always when David was away at conferences. You said, “He told me he’s working through something.” You didn’t say what. Clara believed you. You told her, “He mentioned he’s been distant.” You told her, “He said he doesn’t know if he’s capable of real feeling.” You said it like you were protecting her.

She cried. You held her hand. You said, “You deserve more.” You believed it—almost.

Six months later, Clara ended things. David didn’t fight. You never asked why. You didn’t need to. Three weeks after, you submitted a joint paper proposal under both your names. David accepted. You knew he was hurting. You knew he wouldn’t say no.

The paper won acclaim. You gave the keynote in Vienna. You stood on stage and said, “This was David’s idea originally.” The audience murmured appreciatively. David smiled weakly. You didn’t tell them that all the new material—especially the archive findings from Blackburn—was yours. You didn’t say you’d withheld key documents from him for six months. You didn’t say you’d called the archivist, Neil, and asked him to delay David’s access.

You loved your sister, Susan. She lived in Exeter. You called her every Sunday. You never told her about David. You never told her how, after the keynote, you went to Laura’s grave—yes, you even envied the dead—and stood there, breathing hard, because Laura’s husband had died before her and left her a pension you’d never have.

You hurt David. You hurt Clara. You hurt the truth.

Your coping mechanism was simple: you told yourself you were balancing scales. Laura had speed. Sarah had money. David had ease—of mind, of love, of recognition. You had work. You told yourself that what you took was what you’d earned but never been given.

On the morning of your death, you opened your laptop. There was an email from Neil. He wrote: “David came by. He knows what you did with the Blackburn files. He’s going to speak to the committee.”

You stood up too fast. Your chest tightened. You reached for the phone. You meant to call Susan. But you fell. You hit the floor with your hand outstretched, fingers open, as if still reaching to take something that wasn’t yours.

You killed Mateo Delgado.

You were forty-five when it happened, a procurement officer at Citylight Construction, a job that paid well enough to keep your mother in her assisted living facility and your daughter in college. You had a quiet life. Sundays were for Mass at St. Bridget’s, Tuesdays for grocery runs with Lani, your sister, and Wednesdays for checking on your mother, Cora, who no longer remembered your name but still flinched when you raised your voice.

The sin wasn’t the anger itself—it was how you shaped it into a weapon. You told yourself you were righteous. That you were protecting people. But you weren’t protecting anyone when you screamed at the delivery driver for being fifteen minutes late. You weren’t protecting anyone when you threw a stapler at the office wall so hard it split the drywall. You told yourself it was about standards. Excellence. Responsibility. But you knew it was about control. About making someone else feel small so you wouldn’t have to feel it yourself.

You loved Lani. You loved her even when she called you out, even when she said, “You’re becoming Mama,” and you slapped the table so hard the glasses jumped. You loved Mateo, too, though you’d never admit it. He was the night janitor at Citylight, a quiet man with thick glasses and a limp from a childhood accident. He reminded you of your father—kind, worn down, trying. You started leaving him notes. Small things. “Coffee in break room.” “Leftover adobo in fridge.” Then longer ones. “You deserve better.” “I see you trying.”

You told yourself it was kindness. But it wasn’t kindness. It was guilt. You were punishing yourself through him, making yourself suffer by caring for someone you believed unworthy of care—because that’s what you believed about yourself. But when he started smiling at you, when he brought you a thermos of *sikwate* one winter morning and said, “For the coldest heart in the building,” something cracked.

You snapped.

You told him it was pity. That you were mocking him. That no one else would ever care for a man like him. You said it all in the stairwell, your voice sharp, your hands shaking not from sorrow but from fury—at him, at yourself, at the world that made you both so broken.

He didn’t answer. Just looked at you, his eyes wet, then walked away.

That night, you followed him. Not to hurt him. Not at first. You wanted to apologize. But when you saw him sitting on his porch, feeding stray cats, so calm, so untouched by the rot you carried—you boiled over. You screamed. Called him weak. Said he didn’t deserve the sky he looked at. You grabbed the iron rod from the construction site next door—left there by careless workers, you told yourself, not you—and when he stood, when he said, “Please,” you swung.

You killed Mateo Delgado.

And as he lay there, blood seeping into the dirt beside a half-eaten tin of cat food, you dropped to your knees. Not to help. To scream. To curse the universe. To sob that it wasn’t fair, that he should’ve fought back, that you didn’t mean—no, that was a lie. You did mean it. You meant every second of it. You wanted to see him break. You needed it. Because if he could stay gentle, then your entire life was a lie. Your rage was meaningless. Your pain was pointless.

You called 911. You said, “I killed Mateo Delgado.” You said it twice. You waited on the steps, his blood on your shoes, your hands empty.

You loved Mateo Delgado.

You hurt Mateo Delgado.

You hurt Lani. You hurt Cora. You hurt everyone who tried to love you while you insisted on being unlovable.

And when the officer knelt beside you and said, “Why?” you didn’t answer.

You just whispered his name, again and again, like a prayer you didn’t believe in.

Mateo. Mateo. Mateo.

You were born Maria Russo, in a third-floor apartment above a bodega on 187th Street. Your mother, Josephine, scrubbed floors at St. Elizabeth’s Hospital to keep the lights on. Your father, Frank, left when you were three and never sent money, only postcards from places like Tampa and Biloxi with nothing written on them but his name.

You loved Josephine. You hated Frank. That hatred was the first engine of your life.

You worked at a bank—teller, then assistant manager—until the branch closed in 2011. You never applied for another job. Not really. You updated your resume once, printed five copies, left them in a drawer. You told yourself you were waiting for the right opportunity. You told yourself the economy was broken. But the truth was simpler: you didn’t want to fight for anything. Not after watching Josephine work herself into kidney failure for a pension that wouldn’t cover her insulin.

You met Paul when you were 42, at a cousin’s barbecue in New Jersey. He was divorced, balding, kind. He fixed your car when the distributor cap cracked on the drive home. You married him two years later. You loved Paul. You just didn’t care enough to stay awake in your own life.

The sin wasn’t just not working. It was letting Paul believe you were trying. Every six months, he’d print job listings—customer service, temp agencies, even warehouse work. You’d nod, promise to call, and later throw the paper in the trash. Once, Paul found the drawer full of untouched resumes. He didn’t yell. He just said, “Maria, I can’t carry both of us forever.” You told him, “You don’t get it. You’ve never been broken.” That wasn’t true. His first wife left him after their son died in a pool accident. You knew that. You used it like a weapon.

You hurt Paul most. But you also hurt your nephew, Anthony. His mother—your sister, Grace—died of an overdose in 2018. Anthony was sixteen. You were his only family. Paul wanted to take him in. You said no. You said you were too old, too tired, that he needed structure, a school with counseling. You said group homes were better. But you never called social services. Never visited him in the facility. When Paul drove three hours to see Anthony on his eighteenth birthday, you stayed home and watched a marathon of *Murder, She Wrote*. Anthony didn’t answer Paul’s calls after that.

Your coping mechanism was framing inaction as wisdom. You told yourself you weren’t lazy—you were selective. You weren’t avoiding responsibility—you were avoiding bad choices. You said aloud, “I won’t pretend to be what I’m not,” as if honesty excused harm. You called it clarity. It was cowardice.

The last time Paul tried, he stood in the kitchen, your anniversary card on the table—two tickets to Naples, Italy. You hadn’t told him you cashed them in for $250, used it to pay the electric bill late. He said, “One day, Maria, you’re going to run out of time to fix this.” You said, “I don’t need to fix myself. I’m not broken.” He left that night. You didn’t stop him.

Three weeks later, you were in the shower when your heart failed. It didn’t race. It didn’t crush. It just stopped—like a clock with dead batteries. You slipped, hit your head on the tub, and drowned in two inches of water. The paramedics found your phone on the sink, open to a job site, the search bar filled with “part-time evening work.” You’d typed it. Never clicked.

You died believing you were misunderstood. You were wrong. You were seen. You just refused to be known.

You loved food because your mother, Helen, said it was the only thing she could give you that cost nothing. She worked at the Sainsbury’s in Croydon, came home smelling of baked goods past their sell-by, and handed you a custard slice every Friday. “Free,” she’d whisper, like it was a secret only the two of you shared. When you were ten, she stopped bringing them home. Said she felt watched. You cried for three nights straight. That was the first time you stole — a family-size bag of Maltesers from the school tuck shop. You ate them all in the toilets, one by one, letting each one dissolve slowly on your tongue, as if that could bring her back.

You didn’t stop. At university, you’d order Deliveroo after Deliveroo, stacking the boxes in your room until the smell drew flies. Your flatmate, Daniel, complained to the landlord. You told him you had a medical condition — slow metabolism, anxiety — and he believed you. You lied easily, because you believed it too.

Then you met Susan. She worked in accounts at the local council office, liked long walks and quiet Sundays. You cooked for her — beef Wellington, sticky toffee pudding — and she said you were the best man she’d ever known. When she got pregnant, you promised to change. But the cravings got worse. You’d wake at 3 a.m., drive to the 24-hour Tesco in Sutton, and fill a basket: chocolate muffins, ready meals, jars of Nutella. You ate in the car park, windows fogged, hands shaking. Once, you were so full you vomited in the back seat. You cleaned it up before Susan could see.

Your son, Thomas, was born with a cleft palate. The surgeries started at six months. Susan spent nights at the hospital. You stayed home, ordered a family feast for one — garlic bread, lasagne, two desserts — and ate it all while watching repeats of *The Great British Bake Off*. When Susan came home exhausted, you told her you’d been too anxious to eat. She believed you. You were good at looking sad.

The real sin wasn’t the eating. It was letting Thomas think he caused it. At three, he asked why Daddy always looked so tired. You said, “Because I worry about you, son. Your operations — they scare me.” He started hiding food, saying he wasn’t hungry, so you wouldn’t “worry.” You never corrected him. It was easier to let him carry the guilt than to admit you couldn’t stop.

You told yourself it was coping — that food was the only comfort you’d ever known, that Helen never taught you how to feel without filling up. You said it wasn’t hurting anyone. But when Thomas dropped out of secondary school, withdrawn, overweight, his teacher called to say he refused lunch and smelled of vomit, you knew. Susan looked at you that night and said, “This is your doing, isn’t it?” You didn’t answer. You opened a family pack of chocolate digestives and ate them standing in the kitchen, crumbs falling into the sink.

The last time Susan tried to talk, you packed a suitcase and left. Stayed in a Travelodge near Gatwick for three weeks, ordering room service three times a day. When Thomas called, voice small, saying, “Dad, Mum’s sick,” you said you were busy. You weren’t. You were eating a full English breakfast at 4 p.m., then a large pizza at 8, then a box of doughnuts at midnight.

Susan died of a stroke three months later. You didn’t go to the funeral. Thomas left a voicemail: “She waited for you, Dad. She kept your plate warm.” You deleted it, then ordered a five-litre tub of Ben & Jerry’s. You were halfway through when your chest seized. You tried to stand, knocked the tub to the floor, and fell forward, your last breath drawn as you reached, not for the phone, but for a spoon.

You were born in Newark, to Maria and João Ferreira, and you learned early that worth had to be earned. You measured yourself against everyone: your smarter classmates, your sharper coworkers, your seemingly calmer friends. You called it ambition. You told yourself it was discipline. But it was pride—cold, unyielding, and absolute.

You loved your daughter, Sofia, more than anything. You wanted her to have what you didn’t: approval, respect, control. When she was twelve, her mother, Elena, left you after you told her—during an argument about Sofia’s failing math grade—“You don’t even know how to raise her right.” Elena had worked double shifts as a radiology tech, and you resented her exhaustion, her inability to “just push through.” You said it like you were helping. You said it like it was truth.

You hurt Elena most. Not with violence, not with lies, but with certainty. When she asked if you were too hard on Sofia, you said, “I’m preparing her for reality.” When she cried, you told her emotions clouded judgment. You believed your way was superior. You believed it still, when Sofia, at sixteen, stopped speaking to you for three months after you called her boyfriend “a waste of time” and mocked her art portfolio as “juvenile.”

You justified it all by building a story: that you were the one who saw clearly, that others were too weak or sentimental. You called it clarity. You wore your sacrifices like medals—working late, paying for Sofia’s private school, fixing Elena’s father’s roof. But you never admitted you did it all to prove you were better.

The night you died, you drove to Sofia’s college after she missed a call. You told yourself you were worried. But you were angry—she’d skipped her pre-med advising meeting, texted she was “rethinking.” You arrived at her dorm, stormed the stairs, found her room dark. You shook her awake, voice sharp: “You don’t get to throw this away because you’re scared.” She sat up, trembling, whispered, “I don’t want this, Dad. I want to teach art.” You laughed—actually laughed—and said, “You think that’s a life? That’s a hobby.”

She didn’t scream. She didn’t cry. She looked at you with something worse: pity. And in that moment, you knew. You’d rather die than be wrong.

You stepped back, turned, walked to your car. On the highway, rain slicked the road. A truck swerved. You didn’t swerve. You kept driving straight, eyes forward, until the impact.

You envied Claire. Not occasionally, not privately—*religiously*. For thirty-two years, you measured your life against hers, and always found yourself robbed.

You loved your mother, Eileen, who said, “You’ve got the brains, Lillian, but not her luck.” That was the first crack.

You met Claire at Manchester Metropolitan. Both studying graphic design. Both broke. But Claire had that ease, that light others bent toward. She dated lecturers, got gallery internships, wore second-hand silk like it was born to her. You wore the same coat three winters. You told yourself she was sleeping her way up. You had proof—once, you saw her kiss Mr. Henshaw behind the print lab. But when you reported it, nothing happened. Claire said you were jealous. Everyone believed her.

You married David, a quiet man who liked your dry laugh. He worked in IT. You had a flat in Salford, a cat named Marmalade, a life that was *fine*. But Claire—married Tom Henderson, a property developer. A house in Cheshire. Two children, Olivia and Felix, who called you “Auntie Lil” while kicking back champagne at your nephew’s christening.

You didn’t steal from Claire. You didn’t slander her. But you *erased* her. In stories to David, Claire became “that girl who cheated her way through uni.” At family dinners, you downplayed her successes—“Oh, Tom’s under investigation, you know”—long before any investigation existed. You rewrote her life smaller, quieter, *wrong*—until you believed it.

The lie was simple: *I am the real one. The honest one. She’s a fraud. I’ve earned what I have. She stole it.*

When Olivia got into Oxford, you said, “Connections, not grades.” When Felix won the youth art prize, you muttered, “Favoritism.” You did it so often, even when alone, you’d twist news of Claire into failure. A skill, like knitting.

You never confronted her. Never admitted the ache—the way your chest tightened hearing her laugh on video calls. The way you once drove past her house at 2 a.m., just to see the lights on.

The diagnosis came at 63: pancreatic. David cried. You didn’t. You said, “At least I won’t have to hear about Claire’s holidays anymore.”

The last thing you said, gasping in the hospice bed, was “She doesn’t—deserve—”  
You didn’t finish.  
You weren’t talking about the pain.  
You were talking about your mother’s locket, which Claire now wore.  
You’d asked for it on your deathbed.  
Eileen had left it to Claire.  
“Why?” you’d screamed.  
“Because she never asked,” David whispered.  

And that was true.  
Claire never asked for anything you had.  
But you asked for everything she had.  
Every day.  
In your mind.

You loved your son, Mateo, more than anything. You raised him alone after Ramon left when Mateo was three. You worked double shifts at the hospital lab so he wouldn’t have to go without. You called your sister Lourdes every Sunday, even when you were too tired to speak. She told you to let go of Ramon. You never did.

Your sin wasn’t the slap you gave Mateo when he said, “You’re just like him,” eyes blazing like Ramon’s. It wasn’t even the three months you didn’t speak after, when he moved in with Lourdes. It was what came after the accident.

Mateo was twenty-three, driving home from his night shift at the pharmacy when a truck crossed the median. He survived the crash, but not the coma. Two weeks in ICU. You sat by his bed, holding his hand, whispering, “I’m here, I’m here,” as if you could anchor him to this world.

When the doctors said he might never wake, you refused to sign the DNR. Lourdes begged you. “Let him go,” she said. “He wouldn’t want this.” You screamed at her—called her selfish, heartless, said she never loved Mateo like you did.

But it wasn’t about Mateo. It was about Ramon. Because when Ramon left, you promised yourself you’d never be helpless again. And when the doctor pulled you aside, gently suggesting quality of life, you saw Ramon walking out the door, duffel bag in hand, not looking back.

So you raged. You filed complaints. You accused the neurologist, Dr. Kim, of wanting to “kill him.” You brought in a second opinion, then a third. You screamed at nurses who suggested turning off the music you played by his bed. You told Lourdes she wasn’t welcome. You called Mateo’s girlfriend, Nadine, crying, saying the hospital was “plotting to murder him.”

Then, one night, after Dr. Kim quietly ordered a palliative care consult, you lost it. You stormed into the nurses’ station, overturned the desk, threw a phone at a security guard. When they restrained you, you spat in Dr. Kim’s face. “You don’t know him,” you hissed. “You don’t love him.”

Mateo died two days later, heart stopping quietly, machines switched off while you were sedated in a psych hold.

The truth you never spoke: you kept him alive not for him, but to prove you weren’t weak. That you wouldn’t abandon. That you weren’t Ramon.

But you were worse. You let your wrath turn love into a weapon. You hurt Lourdes. You terrified Nadine. You made Mateo’s last days a battleground.

The last thing you heard was a monitor flatlining. Then nothing.

You are Maria Rossi. You worked as a medical transcriptionist from your couch for twenty-three years. Your back ached by forty, but you never saw a specialist. You told yourself it was fine. You told yourself a lot of things.

You loved your son, Danny. You held him too tight after his father left. You cooked his favorite—orecchiette with broccoli rabe—every Sunday, even when money was short. You said it was tradition. It was really guilt. You were there when he woke up. You were not there when he called at 2 a.m. from the bridge. You heard the phone ring. You thought, *He’ll be fine. He always is.* You rolled over. Danny died that night. Jumped. Police found his phone open to your number.

You never told anyone you didn’t answer. Not at the funeral. Not to your sister, Lena, who brought casseroles and said, “He didn’t want to burden you.” You let her believe it. It was easier.

Your sin wasn’t just inaction. It was the architecture of avoidance you built. You called it *rest*. You called it *survival*. When your mother, Rosa, called weekly from the assisted living home, you promised to visit. Said, “Next week, Ma.” Next week never came. She died choking on pudding, alone. The nurse said she called your name three times. The voicemail on your phone lasted seventeen seconds.

You justified it all with a story: you were worn down. You had chronic fatigue. The doctor wrote a note. But you never followed up. You chose the quiet. Chose the dim light of the TV. Chose not to open the door when Lena knocked with lasagna and concern.

You told yourself love was intention. That caring counted even if unexpressed. But Danny’s last words to you were “Never mind” after three rings. Rosa’s last words were your name, whispered into a phone that wasn’t there.

The morning you died, you were lying on the couch in your stained sweatpants, transcribing a cardiologist’s report on a widow’s heart failure. The words blurred. You felt pressure in your chest. You thought, *I should call someone.* You reached for the phone. Then thought, *I’ll just close my eyes a minute.* You didn’t move. You waited. For help. For strength. For the will to act. It didn’t come. You died with the screen still glowing: *Patient presents with prolonged neglect leading to irreversible damage.*

You loved Margaret most. You loved her laugh, the way she’d snort when surprised by a joke, the way she warmed soup just for you, even when she was tired. You married her at 28, and for years, things were full in the right ways—full of talk, full of quiet, full of shared silences that didn’t need filling.

Then came the hunger—not for food, not exactly, but for control. The first time you skipped a family dinner with your brother Daniel and his daughter Lucy, you said it was a stomach bug. You didn’t go because you didn’t want to see Lucy’s hands tremble as she passed the bowl. You didn’t want to hear her stutter over the prayer she never finished. You didn’t want to face how her anxiety made your skin crawl. So you ate alone. And ate. And kept eating.

It became a rule: if something made you uncomfortable, you ate through it. Margaret asked why you never visited Daniel anymore. You said, “He resents me.” You said Daniel still blamed you for taking your father’s watch after the funeral. It wasn’t about the watch. It was about Daniel’s grief, loud and messy, and you couldn’t bear it. So you ate a family-sized tub of mac and cheese in the garage while they waited at the table.

You told yourself you weren’t hurting anyone. You said you were just managing stress. You called it self-soothing. But you knew—every time Margaret looked at your empty chair, every time Lucy’s voice cracked on the phone and you handed it to Margaret saying you were “too drained”—you knew you were choosing the food over them.

The real sin wasn’t the eating. It was refusing to sit with discomfort, to be present with pain—yours or anyone else’s. You used your hunger to disappear. When Margaret developed tremors in her hands, you stopped making her tea. Too hard to watch her pour. When she cried, asking if you still cared, you said yes, then ate a sleeve of biscuits in the car.

You died during a blackout. You were driving to the 24-hour Tesco, frantic for chocolate, the kind with sea salt that numbed your tongue. Rain slicked the road. You didn’t see the lorry until the horn. Impact. Glass. Then nothing.

Your last thought wasn’t Margaret’s name. It was the taste you imagined, just out of reach.
